facts.claim: HTTP caching (RFC 9111) calls a stored response fresh while its age has not yet passed its freshness lifetime, the time from when the origin made it to when it expires.
A max-age directive tells a cache to treat the response as stale once its age is greater than that many seconds (RFC 9111).
A cache must not serve a stale response unless it is cut off from the origin or a directive allows it (RFC 9111).
MDN: there is no way to delete responses that an intermediate cache stored with a long max-age; a CDN that offers purging lets you cache aggressively and purge only when the content changes.
MDN: for content that changes, common practice is to change the URL each time it changes, often with a version number or hash, so each URL can be cached for a long time.
RFC 9111 allows a cache to collapse requests: combine several incoming requests into a single request to the origin on a miss.
Fastly’s documentation describes request collapsing: one request goes to the origin, the others wait on a waiting list, and the one response is cached and served to all of them.
RFC 5861’s stale-while-revalidate lets a cache serve a response for a set number of seconds after it goes stale, while it revalidates in the background without making the client wait.
Anthropic: a prompt cache entry lives 5 minutes by default, and each use refreshes it at no extra cost.
Anthropic: a prompt cache hit needs the prompt to be 100% identical up to and including the block marked for caching.
Serving a language model keeps a key-value (KV) cache for each request, which grows and shrinks as the request runs (Kwon et al., 2023, the vLLM paper).
